title: Haggai

stories.title: 🏗️ Haggai 1
summaryBullets: In the second year of the reign of Darius, on the first day of the sixth month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, stating (1:1).
that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “These people say, ‘The time has not yet come to rebuild the house of the LORD.’” (1:2).
Then the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet, saying: (1:3).
“Is it a time for you yourselves to live in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?” (1:4).
Now this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Consider carefully your ways. (1:5).

You have planted much but harvested little. You eat but never have enough. You drink but never have your fill. You put on clothes but never get warm. You earn wages to put into a bag pierced through.” (1:6).
This is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Consider carefully your ways. (1:7).
Go up into the hills, bring down lumber, and build the house, so that I may take pleasure in it and be glorified, says the LORD. (1:8).

You expected much, but behold, it amounted to little. And what you brought home, I blew away. Why? declares the LORD of Hosts. Because My house still lies in ruins, while each of you is busy with his own house. (1:9).
Therefore, on account of you the heavens have withheld their dew and the earth has withheld its crops. (1:10).
I have summoned a drought on the fields and on the mountains, on the grain, new wine, and oil, and on whatever the ground yields, on man and beast, and on all the labor of your hands.” (1:11).

Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God and the words of the prophet Haggai, because the LORD their God had sent him. So the people feared the LORD. (1:12).
Haggai, the messenger of the LORD, delivered the message of the LORD to the people: “I am with you,” declares the LORD. (1:13).

So the LORD stirred the spirit of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, as well as the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and began the work on the house of the LORD of Hosts, their God, (1:14).
on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month, in the second year of King Darius. (1:15).
crossRefs: Ezra 4:24; Ezra 5:1-2; Ezra 6:14-15: Historical frame for the rebuild under Darius.
Deuteronomy 28:22-24: Drought and lack as covenant warnings.
Zechariah 4:6-10: Contemporary encouragement to Zerubbabel: “Not by might…”.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: בָּתִּים סְפוּנִים (batim sefūnim), Greek (LXX): οἶκοι κοιλιοστρεφεῖς/κεκαλυμμένοι (var.), Aramaic: בתין מסופנין
translationNotes.note: Finished/lined houses implying personal comfort while the temple sits in ruins (1:4).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שִׂימוּ לְבַבְכֶם (sīmū levavkhem, ‘set your heart’), Greek (LXX): θέντες ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ ὑμῶν, Aramaic: שימו על לבכון
translationNotes.note: Idiomatic call to weigh one’s life and choices before God (1:5-7).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: אֲנִי אִתְּכֶם (ʾani ʾitkhem), Greek (LXX): ἐγώ εἰμι μεθ’ ὑμῶν, Aramaic: אנא עמכון
translationNotes.note: Covenant presence pledged to empower the work (1:13).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חֹרֶב (ḥōrev), Greek (LXX): αὐχμὸς/ξηρασία, Aramaic: חרבא
translationNotes.note: Named as divinely summoned to frustrate self-focused labor (1:11).

stories.keyTakeaway: God confronts misplaced priorities, explains the drought, promises His presence, and stirs leaders and people to restart the temple work.

headings.text: A Call to Rebuild the Temple

stories.title: ✨ Haggai 2
summaryBullets: On the twenty-first day of the seventh month, the word of the LORD came through Haggai the prophet, saying: (2:1).
“Speak to Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and also to the remnant of the people. Ask them, (2:2).
‘Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? How does it look to you now? Does it not appear to you like nothing in comparison?’ (2:3).

But now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares the LORD. Be strong, O Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. And be strong, all you people of the land, declares the LORD. Work! For I am with you, declares the LORD of Hosts. (2:4).
This is the promise I made to you when you came out of Egypt. And My Spirit remains among you; do not be afraid.” (2:5).
For this is what the LORD of Hosts says: “Once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth, the sea and the dry land. (2:6).
I will shake all the nations, and they will come with all their treasures, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of Hosts. (2:7).
The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine, declares the LORD of Hosts. (2:8).
The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former, says the LORD of Hosts. And in this place I will provide peace, declares the LORD of Hosts.” (2:9).
On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to Haggai the prophet, saying, (2:10).
“This is what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Ask the priests for a ruling. (2:11).
If a man carries consecrated meat in the fold of his garment, and it touches bread, stew, wine, oil, or any other food, does that item become holy?’” “No,” replied the priests. (2:12).
So Haggai asked, “If one who is defiled by contact with a corpse touches any of these, does it become defiled?” “Yes, it becomes defiled,” the priests answered. (2:13).
Then Haggai replied, “So it is with this people and this nation before Me, declares the LORD, and so it is with every work of their hands; whatever they offer there is defiled. (2:14).
Now consider carefully from this day forward: Before one stone was placed on another in the temple of the LORD, (2:15).
from that time, when one came expecting a heap of twenty ephahs of grain, there were but ten. When one came to the winepress to draw out fifty baths, there were but twenty. (2:16).
I struck you— all the work of your hands— with blight, mildew, and hail, but you did not turn to Me, declares the LORD. (2:17).
Consider carefully from this day forward — from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, the day the foundation of the LORD’s temple was laid — consider carefully: (2:18).
Is there still seed in the barn? The vine, the fig, the pomegranate, and the olive tree have not yet yielded fruit. But from this day on, I will bless you.” (2:19).
For the second time that day, the twenty-fourth day of the month, the word of the LORD came to Haggai, saying, (2:20).
“Tell Zerubbabel governor of Judah that I am about to shake the heavens and the earth: (2:21).

I will overturn royal thrones and destroy the power of the kingdoms of the nations. I will overturn chariots and their riders; horses and their riders will fall, each by the sword of his brother. (2:22).

On that day, declares the LORD of Hosts, I will take you, My servant, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, declares the LORD, and I will make you like My signet ring, for I have chosen you, declares the LORD of Hosts.” (2:23).
crossRefs: 1 Kings 6-8: Former temple built and dedicated by Solomon.
Hebrews 12:26-28: “Yet once more” shaking cited later.
Isaiah 60:5-11: Nations’ wealth coming to Zion (treasure influx theme).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: חִזְקוּ… רוּחִי עֹמֶדֶת (ḥizqū… rūḥi ʿomedet), Greek (LXX): ἰσχύετε… τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἑστήρικται, Aramaic: אתחסנו… רוחי קיימא
translationNotes.note: Covenant reassurance matching earlier promises of presence (2:4-5).

translationNotes.term: Shake the heavens and the earth
translationNotes.original: Hebrew: מַרְעִישׁ (marʿīsh) imagery, Greek (LXX): σείσω τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, Aramaic: אזיע שמיא וארעא
Hebrew: חֶמְדַּת כָּל־הַגּוֹיִם (hemdat kol-haggoyim, ‘treasure/valued things,’ plural sense), Greek (LXX): τὰ ἐκλεκτὰ πάντων τῶν ἐθνῶν, Aramaic: חמדת כל עממיא
translationNotes.note: Here best read as wealth/goods flowing in, not a messianic title (2:7-8).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: שָׁלוֹם (shalom), Greek (LXX): εἰρήνη, Aramaic: שלמא
translationNotes.note: Wholeness and well-being promised “in this place” (2:9).

stories.keyTakeaway: God tells the discouraged remnant to be strong and work, for he is with them and his Spirit remains; he will shake the heavens, the earth, and all nations, fill the house with treasure and glory greater than the former, and grant peace. A priestly ruling shows the people’s defilement spread to their offerings, yet from the day the temple’s foundation is laid God will bless them; he will overturn royal thrones and make Zerubbabel his servant like a signet ring, for he has chosen him.

headings.text: The Coming Glory of God’s House

intro:
Haggai was written by Haggai the prophet (Haggai 1:1; also referenced in Ezra 5:1 and 6:14, where his ministry alongside Zechariah is credited with motivating the rebuilding of the second temple). Of Haggai's personal background, Scripture preserves nothing beyond his name and prophetic office, with no patronymic, village, or tribe given. The book contains four precisely dated oracles, all delivered within a four-month window in the second year of the Persian king Darius I (522-486 BC), placing the entire ministry in the year 520 BC: the first oracle on the first day of the sixth month (Haggai 1:1, August 29, 520 BC), the second on the twenty-first day of the seventh month (Haggai 2:1, October 17, 520 BC), and the third and fourth both on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (Haggai 2:10 and 2:20, December 18, 520 BC). This makes Haggai one of the most precisely dated books of the Bible. Haggai 2:3 ("Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory?") may suggest that Haggai himself had seen Solomon's first temple before its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar in 586 BC, which would place his birth before about 596 BC and make him at least seventy-five years old at the time of his ministry. Haggai was a contemporary of the younger prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah, son of Iddo (Zechariah 1:1), whose first prophecy was delivered two months after Haggai's first oracle (October 520 BC). The prophet's name Chaggai (חַגַּי) means "festal" or "festive," from the Hebrew chag ("feast" or "festival"); it may indicate he was born on one of the three pilgrimage festivals (Pesach, Shavuot, or Sukkot).

The historical setting is the early Persian period after the first return of Jewish exiles to Jerusalem. Cyrus the Great's decree of 538 BC had permitted the captives in Babylon to return to Judah and rebuild the temple (2 Chronicles 36:22-23; Ezra 1:1-4). The first wave of returnees, about fifty thousand strong, came under the leadership of Zerubbabel (the Davidic-line governor and grandson of King Jehoiachin) and Joshua son of Jehozadak (the high priest, of the Aaronic line). They arrived in Jerusalem in 538 BC, set up the altar, and laid the temple's foundation in 536 BC (Ezra 3). But local opposition from the Samaritans and other neighboring peoples, combined with the returnees' own discouragement and preoccupation with rebuilding their own houses, brought construction to a halt for sixteen years. The Persian throne had passed from Cyrus (559-530 BC) to Cambyses II (530-522 BC) and then through political chaos to Darius I (522-486 BC), who consolidated Persian rule. In Darius's second year (520 BC), Haggai and Zechariah began preaching, the people resumed building twenty-three days after Haggai's first oracle (Haggai 1:14-15, September 21, 520 BC), and the second temple was completed in 516 BC under Darius I's continued sponsorship (Ezra 6:15). The broader regional setting included Persian campaigns west toward Greece (the prelude to the Persian Wars of 490 BC and 480 BC), Egypt's restive 27th Dynasty under Persian rule, and the rise of the Greek classical period.

Haggai is the thirty-seventh book of the Christian Old Testament and the tenth of the twelve Minor Prophets, the second-shortest book in the Old Testament (after Obadiah). The Hebrew name Chaggai (חַגַּי) is the prophet's own name. Hebrew manuscript fragments of Haggai were among the Dead Sea Scrolls discovered at Qumran (mid-20th century AD), preserved as part of the Twelve Minor Prophets scrolls; the earliest copies date to the 2nd century BC. Hebrews 12:26 quotes Haggai 2:6 ("Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens") and applies the prophecy to the future final shaking of creation at the end of the age.
